name: Fuzz pedal enclosure
notes: Enclosure for a boutique guitar fuzz pedal, 125B-size. Top face: one 3PDT footswitch (12 mm hole) and two pots (7.5 mm holes). 1/4" input and output jacks on the long sides, 9 V DC jack on the top end. Four corner bosses take M3 screws for a flat bottom plate. It gets stomped on stage, so it must be tough, and the finish matters because boutique pedals sell on looks. Retail target around $180.

analysis.productSummary: A 122 × 66 × 39.5 mm hollow enclosure for a 125B-format boutique fuzz pedal, sold to guitarists at ~$180 retail. At 250 units the winning move is CNC work on aluminum — ideally on a bought-in die-cast blank rather than a solid billet.
detectedFeatures: Four corner screw bosses for M3
1/4" jack holes on both long sides
9 V DC jack hole on end wall

pros: Metal shell survives stage stomping and shields the circuit
Six idle mills locally; no mold tooling risk
Powder coat or anodize gives the boutique finish buyers pay for
Easy to revise hole pattern between batches
cons: Hogging a 36 mm cavity from billet wastes ~80% of the stock
Three hole faces means multiple setups unless redesigned
Unit cost 10x injection molding at high volume
Finishing is a separate vendor and lead time

designTweaks.change: Buy off-the-shelf die-cast 125B blanks and CNC only the 12 mm, 7.5 mm and jack holes plus tapped bosses.
designTweaks.why: Removes all cavity roughing; the shop only runs a 2-3 minute drill/tap cycle in a fixture.
designTweaks.impact: Unit cost drops to roughly $9-16 including the blank, ~60% saving at 250 units.

designTweaks.change: Move the 9 V DC jack from the end wall to one of the long sides, alongside the input jack.
designTweaks.why: All side holes then fall in two fixture orientations instead of three.
designTweaks.impact: Removes one setup, about 15-20% off machining time per part.

designTweaks.change: Radius the four internal cavity corners to R6 and make bosses 8 mm diameter, M3 tapped 6 mm deep.
designTweaks.why: A single 12 mm end mill clears the pocket; fat bosses resist stripping under stomp loads.
designTweaks.impact: Fewer tool changes, ~25% faster roughing on billet parts.

pros: Low tooling; fits the $4,000 budget better than steel molds
Color can be cast in, no paint line needed
Silicone molds tolerate the undercut-free shell shape
cons: No RF shielding without conductive paint; fuzz circuits hum
Impact resistance below aluminum for a stomped product
250 units needs ~10 molds; each mold fades after ~25 pulls
Cast M3 threads strip; inserts add labor

designTweaks.change: Add 2-3° draft to the four cavity walls over the 36 mm depth and radius all internal corners to R3.
designTweaks.why: Straight walls tear silicone molds and force slow demolding.
designTweaks.impact: Roughly doubles mold life, cutting tooling spend per 250 parts by ~30%.

designTweaks.change: Redesign the four corner bosses to accept cast-in M3 brass heat-set inserts, 5 mm OD x 6 mm.
designTweaks.why: Urethane threads fail after a few bottom-plate removals.
designTweaks.impact: Eliminates the top warranty failure mode for about $0.60/part.

designTweaks.change: Add a flat 15 x 15 mm masked pad on the inside end wall for the ground lug.
designTweaks.why: Gives conductive shielding paint a reliable electrical tie point.
designTweaks.impact: Makes the plastic option viable for a high-gain circuit.

pros: Cheapest per part once volume arrives
2.5 mm walls and 18% fill are already mold-friendly
Fits the 400 x 350 x 180 mm idle press envelope easily
cons: Tooling is 2-5x the entire stated $4,000 budget
Side jack holes need two slides, adding tool cost
Plastic reads as cheap in the boutique pedal market

designTweaks.change: Put the input and output 1/4" jack holes on the same long wall so only one slide is needed.
designTweaks.why: Each side action adds cost and maintenance to the tool.

designTweaks.change: Core the four corner bosses to 2.5 mm wall and tie them in with 1.5 mm gusset ribs.
designTweaks.why: Solid bosses in a 2.5 mm shell sink and leave visible dimples on the show face.
designTweaks.impact: Removes cosmetic scrap on the top face, the surface that sells the pedal.

designTweaks.change: Apply 1.5° draft to all four cavity walls and add a light texture to the outer faces.
designTweaks.why: Enables a straight-pull core and hides knit lines around the 12 mm switch hole.
designTweaks.impact: Shortens cycle time and reduces polish cost on the cavity.

analysis.topRecommendation: Run 250 CNC'd aluminum enclosures, but start from bought-in die-cast 125B blanks and machine only the holes and bosses — that lands near $9-16 each plus powder coat, inside budget. Switch to a molded or custom die-cast tool only above roughly 2,500-3,000 units a year, when $10k-plus tooling pays back.
risks: The $4,000 budget buys about 100-150 fully billet-machined aluminum enclosures, not 250, so the blank-plus-drill route is effectively mandatory.
Plastic paths need conductive shielding paint and a ground pad, or a high-gain fuzz circuit will pick up noise.
The STL is a plain solid shell: hole positions, footswitch nut clearance and the 3PDT's ~32 mm body depth are unverified against the 36 mm internal height.
No photos were supplied, so the finish spec (anodize, powder coat, screen print) and its cost are unconfirmed.
Cast or printed M3 threads in the corner bosses will strip on stage; brass inserts or tapped aluminum are required.
